title: On AI disclosure on platforms like steam
author: thelonelyemptiness
selftext:
Anyone already published any game or who knows people who did it on steam or any other platform? I've read that steam did something to stop review bomb solely because of AI use on a game development, but I saw some people who created curator profiles just to tag AI use even though steam already does this. 

I fear this could be used in a toxic/hostile way against devs who filled up the form of AI use.   
As I want too to develop games and I deal with this fear and anxiety that sometimes even paralyze me. I know I shouldn't live worrying about what other people might or might not think, but this is hard for me and I usually hold everything all to myself without venting and end up getting sick and not feeling well.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
I am long winded af. I’m sorry. In advance. 

I think “everyone uses AI” misses the actual point. The meaningful distinction isn’t simply whether someone used AI, or even how much of the work AI performed. It’s whether they’re using it to realize their own creative vision or letting it supply the vision, make the decisions, and determine the result.

There’s a difference between someone who brings ideas, sketches, plans, or a concept they actively develop, and someone whose entire contribution is a vague prompt. The first person is thinking about the world, the visual style, the story, the gameplay, how the mechanics interact, and what kind of experience they want the player to have. They review the results, question decisions, reject things that don’t fit, and keep refining and balancing the game. AI might handle a huge amount of the execution, but the person is still meaningfully shaping what gets made.

For example, using AI to generate a starting point for a 3D asset, then refining it in Blender until it matches what you envisioned, is different from accepting whatever ChatGPT generates, feeding that into Meshy, accepting whatever comes out, and having a coding model assemble everything with almost no creative input or evaluation from you. Both workflows involve AI, but “they both used AI” tells us very little about the person’s actual contribution.

And the Blender part isn’t some requirement. I’m not saying you have to personally model objects or write code for your contribution to count. You could direct those revisions through AI, too. The distinction is whether you’re making meaningful decisions about the result, not whether you’re physically doing the work yourself.

I’m completely on board with a future where someone with an incredible creative vision can use AI to bring it to life without needing to personally master every discipline involved in making a game. They could act as the creative director and final reviewer while AI handles the execution. That is still substantial creative involvement, provided they’re actually directing the project rather than just giving themselves the title.

Their vision doesn’t have to be fully formed before they start, either. Brainstorming with AI, exploring suggestions, and developing ideas together can all be part of that process. Choosing, rejecting, combining, and reshaping those ideas is different from rubber-stamping whatever comes out.

What I’m talking about is someone having one AI act as the creative director for another AI, with their own involvement amounting to “make a 3D adventure game like Minecraft but also like GTA. Make no mistakes.” Then they present the result as though they personally conceived and designed everything. That isn’t the same level of authorship or involvement as someone actively directing the game, even if both rely heavily on AI.

Letting AI do the work is not the same as letting AI decide what the work should be.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
Well looks like I found the latter example I made. The person who has Ai do all the work, make all the decision both creative and not and just checks every few days to see how much it cost him in tokens. Take your slop somewhere else

Of course games should be fun. Where did I suggest otherwise?  I’m just going to as**sume you didn’t bother reading my entire comment.** I’m not surprised. 

You said “everyone uses AI.” I explained why that tells us very little about someone’s actual creative contribution. One person makes the creative decisions and uses AI to execute them. Another delegates those decisions too. Either could produce a fun game. That doesn’t make their involvement equivalent.

I explicitly said I support someone using AI for essentially all the execution while they genuinely direct the project. This isn’t an argument against AI, or a claim that doing more manual work automatically makes a better game.

The examples illustrate that distinction. Calling them hypothetical doesn’t address it. “Is this game enjoyable?” and “What did this person actually contribute, and are they representing that honestly?” are different questions.

You’re perfectly entitled to care only about the first which doesn’t make it an answer to the second…

replies.author: Valdaraak
replies.body:
Hell, I've leaned into (mostly because I've been a troll and shitposter most of my life). I have a website that has "slop" in the title. Website design? Claude. One shot. Content? Nothing but my one-shot legally distinct clones of old games, playable in the browser and accompanied by a short, sometimes funny, blurb by me. Short, some buggy, most can be completed, but all what most people would consider slop. Do I care? No.

But I also did it to experiment. What *can* I do with just one short prompt and no access to outside tools? Some of my friends were curious as well and the site was born. In all it's sloppy goodness.

> this fear and anxiety that sometimes even paralyze me

Don't. If it isn't AI, it's going to be some other thing paralyzing you. Haters will always find, or make up, something to hate, you can't let that guide your actions.

If you don't want to expose yourself to that risk, you'll need to find someone to hire you and avoid doxxing yourself. Otherwise, as a solo dev, you'll always find some less-than-kind comments (or directly death threats).
